segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Getting into a boat, he crossed over and came to his own town.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some people brought him a paralyzed man lying on a bed. Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take heart, child; your sins are forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At this some of the scribes said to themselves,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is blaspheming.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up, pick up your bed, and go to your home.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and went off to his home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the crowds saw this, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as he was reclining at table in the house, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he heard this, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Those who are well have no need of a doctor, but those who are sick do.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous but sinners.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples of John came to him and asked,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old cloak, for the patch pulls away from the cloak, and a worse tear results.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins burst, the wine spills out, and the skins are ruined. Instead they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was saying these things to them, an official came and bowed down before him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My daughter has just died. But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus got up and followed him, and so did his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind him and touched the tassel of his cloak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for she was saying to herself,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus turned, saw her, and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the woman was made well from that hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus came to the official’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd in an uproar,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go away, for the girl has not died but is sleeping.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they laughed at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl got up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the report of this went out through that whole region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had gone into the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you believe that I am able to do this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he touched their eyes, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And their eyes were opened. Jesus sternly warned them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “See that no one knows of this.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they went out and spread the news about him through that whole region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going out, people brought to him a mute man possessed by a demon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the demon had been driven out, the mute man spoke. The crowds were amazed and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Pharisees said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus went around all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and cast down, like sheep without a shepherd.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.”

notes.note: This is Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee, where Matthew has said Jesus settled after leaving Nazareth (4:13). The Greek word covers any settlement larger than a village; “town” fits a place of Capernaum’s size better than “city.”

The Greek word is the general term for a child of either sex, used here as an affectionate address. Most English versions have “son” because the person addressed is a man, but Greek has a separate word for “son,” and Matthew did not use it.

This was a station where tolls and customs duties were collected on goods in transit. The collectors worked under contract for the ruling power and were widely suspected of overcharging. Observant Jews therefore classed them with “sinners,” as in verses 10–11.

The Greek does not say whose house this is. The parallel in Luke 5:29 makes it the tax collector’s own house, and most readers assume the same here, but Matthew’s wording could also mean the house where Jesus was living in Capernaum. Diners at a formal meal reclined on couches, hence “reclining at table.”

notes.phrase: I desire mercy and not sacrifice
notes.traditional: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice
notes.note: The quotation is Hosea 6:6, which Jesus cites again at 12:7. “Go and learn” is a teacher’s formula for sending a student back to study a text. The Hebrew word behind “mercy” means loyal, steadfast love, and the Septuagint regularly rendered it with the Greek word used here.

notes.traditional: children of the bridechamber; wedding guests
notes.note: The Greek has a Semitic idiom, literally “sons of the wedding hall,” meaning those who belong to the wedding party. Some take it more narrowly as the bridegroom’s attendants. A wedding was a time of feasting, and fasting was a sign of mourning.

The Greek word covers anyone holding a position of authority, from a king to a local magistrate or community leader. “Ruler” suggests a sovereign to a modern reader, which is not meant. Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 identify the man as a synagogue leader named Jairus. The same word is rendered “ruler” in verse 34, where the head of the demons is meant.

The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself or kneeling before a superior, whether a god, a king, or someone from whom a favour is begged. Older versions have “worshipped,” and Matthew may intend his readers to see more in the gesture than the official did. In the scene itself it is the posture of an urgent petitioner, and many modern versions render it “knelt before him.”

The word can mean the edge of a garment, but it is also the Septuagint’s term for the tassels that Numbers 15:38–39 commands Israelites to wear on the corners of their garments. Matthew uses it in that sense at 23:5. Most scholars think the tassel is meant here, though “edge” remains possible.

The verb in verses 21–22 is the ordinary Greek word for “save” or “rescue,” used of deliverance from illness and danger as well as from sin. A Greek reader would hear both senses in “your faith has made you well.” English cannot keep both in one word, and the context here is healing.
Pipers and wailing mourners were hired for funerals, which took place within hours of death. Their presence shows that the household regarded the girl as dead and that burial preparations had begun.

notes.phrase: By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.
notes.traditional: He casteth out devils through the prince of the devils
notes.note: A few early witnesses, chiefly of the so-called Western text, lack this verse, and some scholars think it was added from 12:24. The great majority of manuscripts include it, and the SBLGNT prints it without brackets.

The verb is the same one used in verses 33–34 for driving out demons and in verse 25 for putting the crowd outside. In this period it could also mean simply “send out” or “bring out” with no idea of force, which is the sense here, though it is a stronger word than the usual verb for sending.

The choice between “gospel” and “good news” recurs in nearly every book and should not vary by chapter.
This very frequent discourse marker is variously rendered “behold,” “look,” “just then” or omitted, and needs a single policy.
Used of synagogue leaders, magistrates, council members and the head of the demons; a decision is needed on when to use “ruler,” “leader” or “official.”
